title: 1997 APMO Problems/Problem 2
text:
Problem[edit]

Find an integer in the range such that is an integer.


Solution[edit]

We proceed by contradiction. Assume there exists an odd integer n > 1 such that n | (2n + 2). Since n is odd, gcd(n, 2) = 1. We can factor out a 2 from the expression and divide it out without altering the divisibility condition: n | 2(2n−1 + 1) =⇒ n | (2n−1 + 1) Let p be any prime factor of n. It follows that p | (2n−1 + 1), which yields the congruence: 2 n−1 ≡ −1 (mod p) Squaring both sides gives 22(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). Because n is an odd number, n − 1 is even. Let us extract the highest power of 2 dividing n − 1. Let n − 1 = 2s · m where m is an odd integer and s ≥ 1. Thus, 2s is the exact highest power of 2 dividing n − 1. Let d be the multiplicative order of 2 modulo p. We know that: 1. d must divide 2(n − 1) = 2s+1m (since 22(n−1) ≡ 1 (mod p)). 2. d cannot divide n − 1 = 2sm (since 2n−1 ≡ −1 (mod p) ̸≡ 1 (mod p)). The only way d divides 2s+1m but fails to divide 2sm is if 2s+1 strictly divides d. Therefore, 2 s+1 | d. By Fermat’s Little Theorem, the order d must divide p − 1. Consequently: 2 s+1 | (p − 1) =⇒ p ≡ 1 (mod 2s+1) This condition must hold for every prime factor p of n. The product of primes that are all congruent to 1 modulo 2s+1 will also be congruent to 1 modulo 2s+1. Therefore, the product itself, n, satisfies: n ≡ 1 (mod 2s+1) This implies 2s+1 | (n − 1), which contradicts our initial definition that 2s is the highest power of 2 dividing n − 1. Thus, our assumption is false. No odd integer n > 1 can satisfy the condition. The integer n must be even. Part 2: Constructing an Even Solution Since n must be even, let n = 2k. Substituting this into our divisibility condition gives: 2k | (22k + 2) =⇒ k | (22k−1 + 1) Because 22k−1 + 1 is an odd number, k must necessarily be an odd integer. We search for a solution where k is the product of two distinct odd primes, p and q. Thus, k = pq. We require: pq | (22pq−1 + 1) This requires the expression to be divisible by both p and q. Step 2.1: Bounding Modulo p By Fermat’s Little Theorem, 2p−1 ≡ 1 (mod p). We reduce the exponent 2pq −1 modulo p − 1: 2pq − 1 = 2q(p − 1) + 2q − 1 ≡ 2q − 1 (mod p − 1) To satisfy the congruence modulo p, we need: 2 2q−1 ≡ −1 (mod p) Let us test the prime p = 11, which gives p − 1 = 10. We need 22q−1 ≡ −1 (mod 11). Since 25 = 32 ≡ −1 (mod 11), we can fulfill this if the exponent is congruent to 5 modulo 10: 2q − 1 ≡ 5 (mod 10) =⇒ 2q ≡ 6 (mod 10) =⇒ q ≡ 3 (mod 5) Step 2.2: Bounding Modulo q Substituting p = 11 into the original exponent gives 22q − 1. We reduce this modulo q − 1: 22q − 1 = 22(q − 1) + 21 ≡ 21 (mod q − 1) We now need divisibility by q: 2 21 ≡ −1 (mod q) =⇒ q | (221 + 1) Using the sum of cubes factorization, we factor 221 + 1: 2 21 + 1 = (27 ) 3 + 1 = (128 + 1)(1282 − 128 + 1) = 129 × 16257 = 3 × 43 × 16257 We require a prime factor q that satisfies the condition q ≡ 3 (mod 5). Testing the prime factor q = 43, we see that 43 ≡ 3 (mod 5) holds perfectly Conclusion We have found two primes p = 11 and q = 43 that satisfy all necessary modular arithmetic constraints. k = p × q = 11 × 43 = 473 n = 2k = 2 × 473 = 946 We check this against the bounds of the problem statement (100 ≤ n ≤ 1997). The value 946 lies strictly within this range. By our construction, 473 | (2945 + 1), which rigorously guarantees that 946 | (2946 + 2). Final Answer: The integer n is 946
